title: The Story the Stones Refuse
aliases: Four Hundred Years and a Bell
The Ear That Was Never Cut
logline: Two colossal standing Buddha figures cut from granite ten kilometres apart, one finished and famous for being the finer, the other stopped part-way with an ear still uncut and no ornament above its head, and one story about a master, a pupil and a bell that everybody is told on arrival and that the stones put four hundred years out of reach.
human_question: If the story that is not what happened is also the reason anybody ever looks carefully at either of these, which one am I supposed to give up?

place.what_kind_of_place: Two dry-zone rock-carving sites about ten kilometres apart on an inland plain of scrub, paddy and granite outcrops. At the first, a standing figure of the Buddha some thirteen metres high with its lotus pedestal has been cut almost in the round from a single granite face and left joined to the cliff behind it by one narrow strip of rock at the back; it stands inside a low enclosure among the scattered worked stone of a brick shrine that no longer exists, and it faces due east across a fifth-century reservoir. At the second, reached by a track through low forest and then seventy-five rock steps, a figure of nearly the same height stands sunk into an alcove in a cliff, framed by the rock, joined to it along the entire height and width of its back and head. That one was never finished: the ornament that should rise above the head was never cut, one ear is incomplete, the robe never received its final polish, and the base under its feet is a plain undressed block of stone with the soles resting on the living rock. Around it is a hermitage: dozens of drip-ledged caves, early inscriptions cut above them, a Bo tree, a second reclining image, and very few visitors. Both figures are in worship. One is on every itinerary. The other is not.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Scale that needs no aerial and no explanation: from the ground, at the foot of a thirteen-metre figure, a human being in the frame is the measurement. Then the light. The finished figure faces the sunrise across open water and the first rays reach it before they reach anything else on that plain; the place-name itself is read locally as meaning sun-eating. Ten kilometres away the other figure stands back inside its alcove in permanent shade, and whatever light reaches it arrives shallow, sideways and briefly, along surfaces that were left rough. And the unfinished surfaces themselves are the strongest close-up material either site offers: chisel marks that run and then simply stop, a blank where an ornament belongs, an ear that is half an ear, a base that is still a block. Sixteen centuries of monsoon and dry-season heat have worked on all of it, and that shows too.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Nothing on either site moves. Everything that changes is light, weather, and people arriving and leaving, none of it under the crew's control. The sun comes up and crosses one face; the shadow cast by a raised palm swings and shortens; in the alcove the light rises up a wall and goes again. Flowers are laid and wilt within a day. Rain arrives hard in the north-east monsoon and the granite goes black and shines. Coaches come to one site and not to the other, so the first is loud by mid-morning and the second is quiet all day.
place.when_it_looks_best: First light, and that is the whole schedule. The east-facing figure is at its best in the few minutes after sunrise on a clear morning, which in the dry zone is most mornings between about February and September. The alcove figure needs the shallow oblique light of early morning or late afternoon, and it is not yet known whether direct sun ever reaches the unfinished ear at all; both answers serve the film. The two sites cannot be shot at one sunrise, and the film does not pretend otherwise: two mornings, ten kilometres apart, which is the argument rather than a compromise.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A dry-zone dawn film about two enormous stone figures and the road between them. Dark to light, one site to the other, finished to unfinished, and a sunrise arriving on a face that has been waiting for it for a very long time. The close work carries the middle: grain, lichen, water-stain, tool marks that stop mid-stroke, an ear that is half cut, a base that is still a block. Somebody with no interest in philosophy gets a complete piece with a build and a payoff, and the scale does the rest.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration of something quite exact, and it never has to contradict anything on screen. There are two accounts of these two objects in circulation. One is a story about a master, a pupil and a bell, told at the gate and remembered by everyone. The other is a pair of scholarly datings four hundred years apart, which makes the competition impossible. The voice does not stage a contest between them, because the sources it is reading would not recognise that contest: a century, a school, a master and a pupil are all names for classes and persons, and the books call that worldly usage. What the film does instead is show the viewer a comparison they can only ever make in memory, hand them the sun arriving on a finished face and then on an uncut ear ten kilometres away, and let them notice that their eyes never held both. That is why the story lived. Nothing could ever contradict it in one look.

sequence.on_screen: Before sunrise. Drone low over still water, turning inland: a plain going from black to grey, granite outcrops, and one upright shape standing clear of the scrub with no light on it yet. Then ground level, wide, the figure against a lightening sky.
sequence.voice: There are two ways of talking about what is in front of you, and the books this series reads keep them apart on purpose. One of them uses the words everybody uses: a being, a person, a tree, a mountain, a river. That one was chosen deliberately, so that people could follow easily. It is not the beginner's version. It is a method.

sequence.on_screen: Ground, close to the base, tilting up the full height: the feet, the pleated robe, the bare right shoulder, the right palm raised open. Then a visitor's shoulders entering frame at the bottom edge, which is the only scale the shot needs.
sequence.voice: Here is what you are told when you arrive. There were two carvers, a master and his pupil, working at the same time on two figures ten kilometres apart, and whoever finished first would ring a bell. The bell rang. The other man put down his tools and never went back. Everyone who comes here is given that story, and it is the reason they then walk round and look at the robe.

sequence.on_screen: The road west. Tarmac, then gravel, then a track: scrub, paddy bunds, a tank, egrets, a single bus. Then low forest and seventy-five rock steps going up, filmed from the bottom so the top is out of sight.
sequence.voice: Ten kilometres. Whatever anyone decides about these two figures, nobody has ever decided it by looking, because they cannot be looked at together. These books say a mind knows one object at a time, and never arises at all without an object. Not one thing after another as a piece of advice about how to work. One object, and then the next one, and that is the whole apparatus you have.

sequence.on_screen: The second figure in its alcove, sunk into the cliff, framed by rock. Then the details, held: the blank above the head where an ornament belongs, the incomplete ear, the robe's unpolished folds, the plain square block under the feet, the whole back of the figure still continuous with the wall behind it.
sequence.voice: Senarath Paranavitana read this one as a work King Mahasena began at the instruction of monks and did not live to see finished. Diran Dohanian, working from the style of the other figure, put it four centuries later, and an inscription found in 1951 agrees with him. On those readings no competition was possible; the two men never overlapped. But look at what those readings are made of. A century is a name for a stretch of time. A school is a name for a class of work. A master and a pupil are names for persons. The books put all of that on the same side of the line, and call it worldly usage.

sequence.on_screen: Macro and near-macro on both sites, cut together: feldspar and quartz in raked light, black lichen, a water-stain running down a shoulder, a run of chisel marks that continues and then stops mid-stroke, the one narrow strip of rock still joining the finished figure to the cliff at its back.
sequence.voice: These books define material things by what can be done to them: whatever cold and heat can alter is material. Sixteen hundred monsoons have been altering this. And neither of these figures ever entirely left the cliff. One is held by a strip of rock at the back you could put your arms around. The other is joined along its whole height. Here, at this one, you can see the stone caught half-way between being a wall and being a figure, which is the most useful object on either site. The books also disagree with each other about whether any of what is ultimately there can be seen by an eye at all, and this film leaves that where they left it.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff. Sunrise at the first site: the low sun clears the water and the finished face goes from grey to gold in about ninety seconds, the raised palm throwing a shadow across the chest. Cut. The same hour, the other morning, at the second site: the same low sun arriving shallow across the alcove wall and reaching, or not reaching, the ear that was never cut.
sequence.voice: There. You have just held both of them, and your eyes did not do it. A mind takes one object, then another, and the run is so quick and so gapless that it passes for a single continuous look. That joining is what carried the story of the bell for centuries. Nothing could ever contradict it in one view, because there has never been one view.

sequence.on_screen: Mid-morning at both sites, filmed from where any visitor stands: bare feet on hot sand, flowers going down on a stone table and wilting by noon, oil lamps, a step being swept, a coach party at one site and an empty terrace at the other. No face is held, nobody is singled out, nothing is asked for.
sequence.voice: Nothing here is a mistake waiting to be corrected. The story of the master, the pupil and the bell is ordinary speech doing exactly the work these books say ordinary speech was chosen for, and it works: it is why people stand at the foot of a rock and study an ear. It is also not what happened. Both of those are true, and you are allowed to keep both. Neither of them is the last word about stone. And the story does not even agree with itself about who won. In one version it was the pupil who finished first.

sequence.on_screen: Last light. The finished figure now lit only on one edge, the plain going blue behind it. Then the alcove, already dark, with the shape of the unfinished head just readable. Then a final wide frame with no figure in it at all: the outcrop, the scrub, the sky.
sequence.voice: The books name four things at the end of all their dividing, and three of them are made: knowing, what comes with knowing, and matter. The fourth is not made at all, and they say plainly that it is reached by a great deal of effort and not by looking. There is no shot of it in this film. There could not be. Everything a camera can bring back belongs on the made side, including this.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the three digests answer the question this place has been asking out loud for a century, and they answer it in a way that is not the obvious one. C001 is the frame, and its real content is easy to get wrong. The Pradeepika divides the teaching into two modes, not into false and true: conventional teaching uses everyday names, being, person, woman, man, tree, mountain, river, so that listeners understand easily [C001-P:L51], and is mapped onto the Sutta collection [C001-P:L47], while ultimate teaching describes aggregates, elements and sense bases [C001-P:L49] which are truly existent and do not change from their own nature into another [C001-P:L53]. The Margaya sorts whatever the mind can take up into what truly exists and what does not [C001-M:L38–L40], calls the second a name for what is held to exist by mere notion [C001-M:L48], and defines the first as what remains when dividing can go no further [C001-M:L50–L52], using a table that is only wood in a particular arrangement [C001-M:L46]. Put that on this site and the film's whole architecture follows: the legend of the bell, the eighth-century attribution, the word master, the word pupil, the word finer, and the number four hundred are every one of them names for classes, periods and persons. None of them crosses the line. The Pradeepika is explicit that the final realities are a non-substantial process known fully by omniscient knowledge rather than by human or divine knowing [C001-P:L59], which is exactly why a dating cannot be cast as the ultimate truth that corrects the myth. C003 then supplies what no other location in the group can stage. Mind is the knowing of an object; it takes one object at a time and never arises without one [C003-P:L33]; and it runs as a stream of extremely brief moments that passes for a single continuous mind because of its speed and the absence of gaps [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L31]. The two figures are ten kilometres apart and cannot be brought into one view, so the comparison that both the legend and the dating depend on has only ever happened in memory. C002 holds the floor under all of it: the ultimates are momentary activities rather than substances [C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3], matter is defined by being altered by opposing conditions such as cold and heat [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], and the fourth reality is not produced by conditions and is realised through great effort rather than seen [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46]. An unfinished colossus is the one object that shows all three at once: stone caught between cliff and figure, a process visibly stopped, and a horizon the camera is told in advance it cannot reach.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the interesting distinction here is not myth against science. If the film let the archaeology stand in for ultimate reality it would have failed the primary digest twice over, once by treating a stylistic dating as paramattha when the Pradeepika says the final realities are not known that way [C001-P:L59], and once by the reading the C001 digest names in its own guards, that this is all just atoms and science already said it. What the pairing actually reveals is that both accounts of these stones are conventional, that the conventional is a deliberate method and not a concession [C001-P:L51], and that within the conventional one account can be checked against an inscription and the other cannot, which is a real difference and still not the difference between name and thing. Then C003 does the thing only this location can do. It shows the viewer the mechanism that let the impossible story survive, and it is not credulity: it is that a mind holds one object at a time [C003-P:L33] and that the appearance of a continuous look is made by speed and gaplessness [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L31]. Everybody who has ever compared these two figures, the pilgrim and the art historian alike, did it in memory. The film's most beautiful frame and its clearest statement of the concept are therefore the same frame, or rather the same cut: first sun on a finished face, and the same sun on an ear that was never cut, joined by an edit because there is no other way to join them.

concept_links.why: This is the location in the group where the source's own distinction is already the local controversy, and the digest supports the link only if the film refuses the flattering version of it. The Pradeepika gives two modes of teaching: everyday names, chosen so that listeners could understand easily, with worldly usage as the boundary conventional teaching does not overstep [C001-P:L51], and ultimate teaching in terms of aggregates, elements and sense bases [C001-P:L49], whose objects are truly existent and do not change from their own nature into another [C001-P:L53]. The Margaya divides whatever the mind can take up into the truly existent and the not truly existent [C001-M:L38–L40], names the second as what is held to exist by mere notion [C001-M:L48], and defines the first as the indivisible end of analysis [C001-M:L50–L52], with a table that is only an arrangement of wood [C001-M:L46]. The legend of the master, the pupil and the bell, and equally the words eighth century, master, finer, and the name of a regional sculptural style, are all on the conventional side of that line. The digest's limits are doing the heaviest work in this film. It names as the easiest misreading of the Margaya's flat wording the slide into nothing is real [C001-M:L44–L48], so the film never suggests the figures or the worship are unreal. It rules out presenting the analysis as atomism or as something science already established, because the Pradeepika describes the final realities as a non-substantial process known fully by omniscient knowledge and not by ordinary human knowing [C001-P:L59]; that single line is what forbids the film from letting carbon, style or scholarship stand in for the ultimate, and it is the reason the archaeology is never staged as the truth that beats the story. It rules out labels are bad, stop naming things, since everyday names were the deliberate method [C001-P:L51], which is why the legend is treated as functioning speech and never as ignorance. It rules out mapping the analysis onto identity or social construction, which is what a film about local myth versus colonial-era scholarship would become. And the digest records that the Margaya's own stakes, including rebirth, unseen beings and the rightness of image worship [C001-M:L5–L17], are the source's and cannot be quietly dropped or presented as observable facts; on a site where both figures are in worship, the film neither endorses nor examines that, it simply does not touch it. The Pradeepika's warning against study for gain or status [C001-P:L31–L37] is the note the whole tone is set to.

This link is the reason the location works rather than a decoration on it. The source defines mind as the knowing of an object, takes one object and one aspect of it at a time, and holds that no mind arises without an object at all [C003-P:L33]; and it describes a beginningless stream of extremely brief moments that appears to be one continuous mind because of its speed and the absence of gaps between them [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L31]. The Margaya's parallel move is that mind is one in its general nature and is divided only so that it can be taught [C003-M:L5]. Two figures ten kilometres apart give that claim a form no studio could build: the comparison on which both the legend and its refutation depend cannot be performed by an eye, only carried in memory, and the film's payoff is an edit that makes the viewer feel the join being made for them. The digest's guards are written into the beats. This is not multitasking is a myth: the one-object teaching concerns extremely brief moments of knowing and not a way of organising work, and beat three says so in its own wording. It is not be present, since the source has the life-continuum minds carrying over an object from the dying moments of a previous life [C003-P:L41–L45]. It is not your mind creates your reality. The author's argument that mind rests on a physical base at the heart rather than the brain [C003-P:L59–L69] is a technical position in commentary that the digest says must not be shown as settled science, and it is absent from this film entirely. The source's quantities, minds beyond counting in a finger-snap [C003-P:L53] and matter lasting seventeen mind-moments [C003-P:L55], are reported as its teaching if used at all and never as measurement.

C002 supplies the materiality the close-up work needs and the ceiling the ending needs. Both sources list four ultimates in the same order [C002-M:L5; C002-P:L27–L30] and describe the conditioned three as activities or forces rather than substances [C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3]. Matter is defined not by what it is made of but by what can be done to it: it is what opposing conditions such as cold and heat alter [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17]. Sixteen centuries of monsoon and dry-season heat on exposed granite is that definition filmed rather than illustrated, and the unfinished figure adds what no finished one can, a mass of stone stopped visibly between being a wall and being an image. The digest's restraints shape the writing directly. The extract names the four great elements without defining them [C002-P:L40] and the digest forbids glossing them from popular assumptions, so the voice never says earth or fire about the rock. The Pradeepika says the ultimates are not visible to the eye [C002-P:L34] while the Margaya says the colour element is [C002-M:L17]; the digest records this as unreconciled and flags it for expert reading, so beat five states that the books disagree and the film leaves it alone, rather than telling the viewer that hardness and colour are what they are really looking at. And the fourth reality is unconditioned, always existing, realised only through the path and great effort [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46], never a calm mood or a peaceful shot; beat eight therefore names it and says outright that there is no frame of it, which is the closing obligation the floor imposes.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a story can be false and still be the thing that makes people look carefully, and that this is not a scandal. That the careful correction of the story is made of names too: centuries, schools, styles, masters, pupils. That the comparison everybody makes between these two objects has never been made by an eye, and that the joining is done somewhere else. And that the thing the books point at underneath all of this is not a better date but stone as something that heat and cold can work on, with a fourth item on their list that the film says plainly it cannot show.
what_must_be_real: Both figures are objects of worship and are filmed as such. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repeated or lit for the camera; no flowers are placed, no lamp is lit and no offering is made at the crew's suggestion. Nobody in frame is presented as credulous, ignorant, devout or attained, and nobody is filmed who could not meaningfully refuse, which at the hermitage site means the resident monastic community is asked through the incumbent and a refusal ends that part of the shoot. Faces are not held; the film's people are backs, feet, hands and scale. The legend is recorded as it is actually told on site, in the teller's own terms, and the film does not correct anybody on camera or off. The unfinished surfaces are filmed as they are and nothing is cleaned, wetted, brushed or relit to make a tool mark read better. The two sunrises are two mornings and the film never implies they are one shot. The datings are attributed to the people who proposed them and are not upgraded into settled fact, and the dispute about which figure is taller is recorded rather than resolved. No reconstruction, no animation of a carver at work, no reenactment of a bell.
position_hint: early in the group, after the film that separates a name from a thing: this is the case where two rival names for the same two objects are both in working use, one checkable and one not, and neither of them reaches the ultimate. It is also the group's first colossal object and its first unfinished one, and the unfinished figure is the best teaching object the whole slate has. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The doctrinal trap this film exists to avoid: writing the legend as conventional truth and the archaeological dating as ultimate truth. The C001 digest forbids it, since the Pradeepika says the final realities are known by omniscient knowledge and not by ordinary human knowing [C001-P:L59], and the digest separately rules out presenting the analysis as something science already established. Any cut, any grade or any line that makes the dating feel like a revelation has broken the film.

Mockery, however light. If the tone ever becomes here is what the ignorant believe, the film has failed the floor as badly as any other breach. The legend is functioning conventional speech and is the reason anyone looks at the ear at all.

Reading the unfinished figure as a defeat, a lesser man's work or a lesson about pride. There is no version of this film in which the pupil failed; the story does not even agree with itself about who won, and the unfinished figure is the most doctrinally useful object on either site precisely because a process is visibly stopped.
Sliding into nothing is real, which the C001 digest names as the easiest misreading of the Margaya's own wording [C001-M:L44–L48]. Neither the stone nor the worship is unreal in these sources.

Settling, by implication, the sources' unresolved disagreement about whether anything ultimate is visible to the eye [C002-P:L34 against C002-M:L17], or glossing the four great elements that the extract names without defining [C002-P:L40].
Turning one object at a time into a productivity line about multitasking, or the pre-dawn quiet into be present. The C003 digest rules out both.
Presenting Nibbana as calm, as a peaceful shot of dusk, or as anything the camera got. The sources make it unconditioned and realised through great effort [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46].
Drifting into an archaeology programme in which the datings are the subject and the concept is a closing thought, or into a heritage travelogue in which the legend is colour.
Consent and dignity at a site that receives coach parties, and at a working hermitage where a small resident community cannot easily refuse a crew that has already climbed the steps.

Naming a king or a chronicler in a way that slides into merit or genius. The voice names Mahasena, Paranavitana and Dohanian as people who proposed readings, and must never narrate anyone's merit, piety or artistic greatness.

Drone permission over two sacred sites is genuinely uncertain and may simply be refused. The film is built so that it survives refusal, because a thirteen-metre figure supplies its own scale from the ground and the payoff is a long-lens sunrise, not an aerial.
The payoff depends on clear first light on two separate mornings and on knowing whether any direct sun reaches the unfinished ear. A clouded eastern horizon on both mornings means returning.
drop_if: The legend turns out not to be in living use at the sites, and can only be obtained by asking somebody to recite it for the camera.
Filming cannot happen at either site without intruding on worship, or without the resident community at the hermitage being put in a position where refusal is not real.

The unfinished surfaces cannot be filmed close enough for the blank above the head, the incomplete ear and the undressed base to read, in which case the film has no second object and the comparison has nothing to land on.
The datings collapse on closer reading into a single vague tradition with nothing checkable behind them, which would leave the film with one account instead of two and no historical thread at all.

connections.note: Four names in living use for one mountain, nobody correcting anybody; then two accounts of two stones where one of them is checkable and the other is not, and still neither reaches the ultimate.
One body of water that is correctly counted as five and as three; two figures that are correctly held to be a pair and correctly held to be four centuries apart. Both films refuse to pick.
A riddle put to a king about whether a name and a thing are separate, and a legend that makes the same question a matter of two objects ten kilometres apart.

A colossal rock-cut figure that is no longer the thing its name reports, next to one that never became the thing its name reports. Keep the two films apart in look: that one is a citadel climb, this one is two still objects and a road.

selection.reason: Relocated onto a site where the history is the argument: a famous legend that the stones put four hundred years out of reach, and an unfinished colossus that shows a process stopped. Stands alone and carries C001 without letting scholarship pose as the ultimate.

review.note: Rewritten from the ground up onto a new location after the southern coastal town and its headland lighthouse were set aside. The old central image is dropped entirely: there is no rotating lens turning a steady lamp into a flash and no whirled torch making a ring of fire anywhere in this film, and the Margaya's ring-of-fire line is no longer cited or used. The title is now The Story the Stones Refuse, with the old title kept as an alias. The film is bound to a verified historical thread: two colossal standing granite Buddha figures about ten kilometres apart, the finished one facing east across a fifth-century reservoir and joined to its cliff by one narrow strip of rock at the back, the other a sunken relief still continuous with the rock wall along its whole height, left unfinished with no ornament above the head, one incomplete ear, an unpolished robe and an undressed block for a base; the universally told legend of a master, a pupil and a bell; and the scholarly datings, Paranavitana's reading of an image begun under Mahasena and Dohanian's eighth-century attribution supported by an inscription found in 1951, which between them make the competition impossible. The film deliberately refuses the obvious reading that the legend is conventional and the dating ultimate: the Pradeepika's line that the final realities are known by omniscient knowledge and not by ordinary human knowing is what blocks it, and both accounts are treated as worldly usage, one checkable and one not. The legend is never mocked and never used as a payoff, and the unfinished figure is never a defeat; the four recorded versions of the story, one of which reverses master and pupil, are held in what_is_certain. C003 now does the real work: the two figures cannot be seen in one view, so the comparison exists only in memory, and the payoff is a cut between first sun on a finished face and the same sun on an ear that was never cut. C002 supplies materiality defined by what cold and heat alter, and names the fourth reality as a horizon the film says outright it cannot show. All three concept links were re-tested against the digests and rewritten, with every bearing does_not_transfer line carried into the link or the risks; no concept added or dropped. Eight beats, each with on_screen and voice. New suggested_location with both sites' coordinates, a historical_thread block holding the rival datings and the sun-alignment claim apart, five confirmed Commons images including two of the unfinished figure, and drone refusal recorded as a live risk the film survives.

suggested_location.name: The Avukana (Aukana) Buddha statue and the Sasseruwa (Ras Vehera / Reswehera) Buddha statue, a pair about 10 km apart

also_known_as.name: Avukana / Aukana
also_known_as.meaning: read locally as 'sun eating', for a figure that faces the sunrise
also_known_as.used_by: the finished figure and its village

also_known_as.meaning: the usual name for the unfinished figure and its site

also_known_as.used_by: the temple itself and its signage

also_known_as.name: Kalasela
also_known_as.meaning: a place named in the Culavamsa under Dhatusena, which some scholars identify with the first site; the site's ancient name is otherwise unknown

suggested_location.region: Anuradhapura District, North Central Province, on the dry-zone plain south-west of the ancient capital near Kekirawa, for the finished figure; the unfinished figure stands about 10 km west, at the Kekirawa–Galgamuwa side of the district boundary, and most sources place it in Galgamuwa, Kurunegala District, North Western Province, while some list it under Anuradhapura District. The boundary attribution is unsettled and is recorded rather than resolved.

secondary_coordinates.note: the unfinished figure in its alcove, about 10.5 km west-south-west of the first, at the monastery site

suggested_location.why_here: Because the argument is already on the ground and has been for a century, and because the two objects are physically incapable of being seen together. Every visitor to either site is told the same story, that a master and his pupil raced to carve two colossal figures and that whoever finished first would ring a bell; the story is why anybody studies the robe or notices the ear. The stones do not permit it. The unfinished figure is read by Paranavitana as an image begun under Mahasena in the late third century, and the finished one is placed by Dohanian in the eighth century on stylistic grounds with an inscription found in 1951 behind him, which puts roughly four hundred years between two men who are supposed to have been in earshot of one bell. That is a story that already turns on the concept's own question, and it will not resolve. The site then hands the film three things no analogy could. First, an unfinished colossus: the ornament above the head never cut, one ear incomplete, the robe never given its final polish, the base still an undressed block and the soles resting on the living rock, with the entire back and head still continuous with the cliff, so a mass of granite is visibly stopped between being a wall and being a figure. Second, the finished figure's east orientation, facing the sunrise across a fifth-century reservoir, with a local reading of the name as sun-eating, so the film's most beautiful frame is first light on a finished face and its clearest statement of the concept is the same light on an ear that was never cut. Third, and decisively, ten kilometres of scrub between them, which means no eye has ever held both and the comparison exists only in memory, which is exactly why an impossible story survived. The scale also means the film does not depend on a drone: at the foot of a thirteen-metre figure, a person in the frame is the measurement.
what_to_film: The finished figure from the ground at first light, wide enough to hold the full height and the enclosure, with a visitor's shoulders at the bottom edge for scale. This is the beautiful frame and the schedule is built around it.
The same sunrise in close-up on the face, the raised right palm and its shadow crossing the chest, in real time over the ninety seconds the light takes to change.
The narrow strip of rock at the back that still joins the finished figure to the cliff, filmed from behind or from the side so that it is unmistakably a strip and not a wall.
The scattered worked stone of the vanished brick shrine around the base, and the lotus pedestal, without narrating a builder.
The road and track between the two sites, in one unbroken move if possible, because the distance is a load-bearing fact and not a transition.
The seventy-five rock steps up to the second site, and the approach through the alcove so that the figure is revealed as sunken into the cliff rather than standing in front of it.

The unfinished evidence, held long and lit only by available light: the blank above the head, the incomplete ear, the unpolished robe folds, the plain square block under the feet, the soles on the living rock, and a run of chisel marks that stops mid-stroke.
The same low sun at the second site on a second morning, reaching, or failing to reach, the uncut ear. Both outcomes serve the payoff cut and neither is simulated.
Granite in raked light on both sites: grain, lichen, water-stain, and the difference between a surface that was polished and a surface that was not.

The hermitage around the second figure at a respectful distance: drip-ledged caves, early inscriptions above them, the Bo tree, the reclining image, and the emptiness that the first site does not have.
Worship as it happens, from where any visitor stands: bare feet, flowers laid and wilting, lamps, a swept step. No faces held, nothing requested, nothing repeated.
Last light leaving both figures, and one final wide frame of the plain with no figure in it, for the closing beat.
suggested_location.access: The finished figure is about 175 km from the capital by road via Kurunegala and Galewela, roughly three and a half hours, or about 56 km from the ancient capital city to the north; the nearest town on the main highway is about 10 km away and there are local buses from it and a morning bus from the cave-temple town to the south. The site is an Archaeological Protected Monument with a ticketed enclosure, an access road and a car park, and facilities improved by the Department of Archaeology and the Civil Defence Force. Ordinary temple conduct applies: shoes off, shoulders covered, legs covered. The unfinished figure is reached from the small town to the west by a secondary road and then about 15 km of minor road, followed by seventy-five rock steps; it is a working monastery rather than a managed monument, so access is through the incumbent and the community's wishes govern everything. A vehicle and roughly forty minutes are needed between the two sites, and there is no route from which both can be seen.
suggested_location.best_time: Sunrise, on a clear morning in the dry season, roughly February to September on this plain; the north-east monsoon between about October and January brings the heaviest rain. Two consecutive clear mornings are needed, one at each site, and the film is written on the assumption that they are two mornings. The finished figure is at its best in the first few minutes after the sun clears the horizon to the east. The unfinished figure sits back in an alcove and never receives full frontal sun; the oblique light of early morning or late afternoon is what the close work needs, and whether direct sun reaches the uncut ear at any hour has not been verified. Mid-morning onward the first site takes coach parties and the second stays quiet, which is itself worth filming.

historical_thread.story: Two colossal standing figures of the Buddha, cut from granite about ten kilometres apart on the same dry-zone plain, are the two largest standing rock-cut Buddha images on the island. The Avukana figure, near Kekirawa in Anuradhapura District, was carved almost in the round from a single granite face and left attached to the cliff behind it by one narrow strip of rock; it faces due east across the Kala Wewa reservoir, and the name Avukana is read locally as 'sun eating' for that reason. It is the one universally described as the finer of the two: the robe's pleats are carved with great delicacy, the right palm is raised in an unusual gesture that writers call asisa rather than the ordinary abhaya mudra, and specks of the gilding it once carried are still reported on the surface. It stands among the scattered stone of a brick image house that no longer exists; a donative inscription on a slab from that image house was found in 1951, and five bronzes of Brahma, Indra, Kuvera, Yama and Varuna were recovered from below the figure's feet. The site's ancient name is unknown, and some scholars have proposed identifying it with the Kalasela of the Culavamsa. The Sasseruwa figure, also called Ras Vehera or Reswehera, stands about ten kilometres west, up seventy-five rock steps, inside a monastery of dozens of drip-ledged caves with twenty-three early Brahmi inscriptions above them, a Bo tree said to descend from the sacred tree at the old capital, and a second, reclining image. It is not a freestanding figure at all: it is a high relief sunk into an alcove, framed by the rock, joined to the wall behind it along the full height and width of its back and head. And it is unfinished from the head to the foot. The ornament that should rise above the head was never cut. One ear is incomplete. The robe never received its final polish and is plainly coarser work than its twin's. The pedestal is a square block of stone that was left undecorated, and the soles of the feet rest on the natural rock with no platform under them. The story told at both sites, to almost everybody who arrives, is that the two figures are the result of a contest between a master sculptor and his pupil, working simultaneously, ten kilometres apart, with the agreement that the first to finish would ring a bell; the bell rang, the loser stopped work where he stood, and that is why one image is complete and the other is not. In the most commonly repeated version the master carved the finished figure and the pupil abandoned the other, and the unfinished figure is what a pupil's defeat looks like. The datings make the contest impossible. Senarath Paranavitana read the unfinished image as a work begun by King Mahasena, in the late third century, at the instruction of the monks of one of the capital's great fraternities, and left incomplete when the king died. Diran K. Dohanian, comparing the finished figure with other images on the island and with work of the Amaravati school, placed it in the eighth century, and the inscription found in 1951 is dated to the eighth century on palaeographic grounds. On those readings roughly four hundred years separate the two carvings, and no two men could have shared a bell. The legend is nonetheless what most visitors are told on arrival, and it is what makes them walk round and look closely at an ear.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: The concept's own question is whether a name and the thing named are separate items, and this place has been arguing about exactly that in public for a century, in two registers at once. The Pradeepika's point is not that ordinary speech is a mistake: it says the Buddha taught in everyday names, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that listeners could understand easily, and it treats worldly usage as a boundary that conventional teaching keeps to rather than a fault it suffers from. The legend of the master, the pupil and the bell is that kind of speech working perfectly. It is compact, memorable, transmissible by anyone to anyone, and it makes its hearer do the one useful thing the site affords, which is to look very carefully at two pieces of stone and compare them. It is also not what happened. The crucial move, and the reason this location is right rather than merely interesting, is that the correction is not the ultimate either. A century is a name for a stretch of time; a school of sculpture is a name for a class of work; master, pupil, finer and taller are names for persons and for judgments about them; four hundred is a number attached to the gap between two names. All of that is on the conventional side of the line the sources draw, and the Pradeepika closes the escape route by saying the final realities are known fully by omniscient knowledge and not by ordinary human knowing. So the film has two accounts of the same two objects, both conventional, one checkable against an inscription and one not, and an ultimate that neither reaches. Then the geography does something no other site could. The two figures are ten kilometres apart and cannot be brought into one field of view, and the sources hold that a mind knows one object at a time and never arises without an object, with the appearance of a continuous look produced by speed and the absence of gaps. Nobody has ever seen both. Every comparison ever made between them, by the pilgrim repeating the legend and by the art historian refuting it, happened in memory. That is the mechanism by which an impossible story stayed alive, and it is not credulity; it is the ordinary architecture of knowing. Finally, the unfinished figure is the single most useful object either site holds, because materiality in these sources is defined by what opposing conditions such as heat and cold can alter, and here a mass of granite has been stopped and left visibly half-way between being a cliff and being an image, with an ear that is half an ear and a base that is still a block. Not a lesser man's failure. A process, arrested, in view.
what_is_certain: Two colossal standing Buddha figures stand about ten kilometres apart on the same plain and are the two largest standing rock-cut Buddha images in Sri Lanka.

The Avukana figure is carved from granite, faces due east, stands on a lotus pedestal, and is attached to the rock behind it by a narrow strip left for support rather than being wholly detached. Sources locate that strip at the back, some specifically at the waist.
The Sasseruwa figure is a high relief sunk into an alcove and joined to the rock along the full height and width of its back and head; it was never freestanding.

The Sasseruwa figure is unfinished, and the incompleteness is documented feature by feature: no siraspata above the head, one incomplete ear, a robe that never received its final polish and is coarser work than its twin's, a pedestal left as an undecorated square block, and the soles resting on the natural rock with no platform.
The two figures differ in hand gesture as well as finish: the finished one is described as asisa mudra, unusual on the island, and the unfinished one as abhaya mudra.

The legend of a master and a pupil carving the two figures in competition, with a bell to signal completion, is recorded at both sites and is what most visitors are told on arrival. A Wikimedia Commons uploader's own file description for the unfinished figure recounts it, which is a small measure of how completely it has become the way the place is known.

The legend exists in at least four recorded variants: that a sculptor practised on the unfinished figure before carving the finished one; that he abandoned the first after a crack opened in the rock; that the master carved the finished figure and the pupil abandoned the other; and that the pupil carved the finished figure and the master abandoned the other. The story does not agree with itself about who won, which is one reason it cannot be read as a lesson about a lesser man.
An inscription recording a donor, on a slab from the image house at the finished figure's site, was found in 1951 and is dated on palaeographic grounds to the eighth century.

Senarath Paranavitana proposed that the unfinished image was begun under King Mahasena, whose reign is given as the late third century, at the instruction of monks, and was left incomplete on his death. Diran K. Dohanian proposed the eighth century for the finished figure on stylistic grounds. On those two readings the carvings are roughly four hundred years apart and the competition is impossible.

The unfinished figure stands within an ancient monastery with dozens of drip-ledged caves, twenty-three early Brahmi inscriptions, a Bo tree and a second reclining image, on a site whose foundation tradition reaches back well before either colossus.
Both figures are in active worship, and the finished one is an Archaeological Protected Monument with a ticketed enclosure and coach access.
what_is_disputed: The date of the finished figure. Tradition and much popular writing give the fifth century and the reign of Dhatusena, who built the reservoir it faces in about 460 CE. Dohanian argued for the eighth century from style, and the 1951 inscription is read as supporting him. Another account dates the donor's script only to somewhere between the fifth and eighth centuries. The film holds the fifth-century tradition and the eighth-century attribution apart and does not choose.

The size of the gap between the two carvings, and therefore how impossible the contest is. The widely repeated figure is 'nearly four hundred years', which follows from pairing Paranavitana's late-third-century reading of the unfinished figure with Dohanian's eighth century for the finished one. If the finished figure is fifth-century instead, the gap shrinks to something closer to a century and a half. Every reading on offer still rules out two contemporaries and one bell, but the number four hundred is a consequence of one particular pairing and is reported as such.

Which figure is taller. The finished one is commonly given as 13 m or 43 ft and described as the tallest, and Wikipedia gives 11.84 m for the figure with over 14 m including the pedestal; the unfinished one is given by one detailed account as 39 ft 3 in, about five inches taller than its twin, and by others as slightly smaller. The claim that either is the larger is unsettled and is not used by the film.

The sun-alignment claim. That the finished figure faces due east across the reservoir is consistently reported and is straightforwardly checkable on the ground. That the first rays strike it at dawn, that this was intended, and that the place-name means 'sun eating' are travel-writing and local-etymology claims of a much weaker kind, repeated across many secondary sources without a primary one behind them. The film uses the orientation, which can be verified, and treats the intention and the etymology as what people say.

Why the unfinished figure was left unfinished. Candidates in the literature include the death of the royal patron before completion, a crack opening in the rock, its use as a trial piece or prototype for the other figure, and the competition of the legend. No account is established, and the film does not adjudicate.

Which district the unfinished figure is in. Most sources place it at Galgamuwa in Kurunegala District, North Western Province; some list it under Anuradhapura District, and at least one Wikipedia entry conflates the site with a differently located temple of a similar name. It sits close to a provincial boundary and the attribution is recorded rather than resolved.
The identification of the finished figure's site with the Kalasela named in the Culavamsa is a scholarly conjecture, and the site's ancient name is otherwise unknown.
Whether the unfinished figure's alcove admits direct sunlight onto the incomplete ear at any hour, which the payoff cut is designed around and which is unverified from desk research.

suggested_location.research_note: Everything here is desk research carried out on 25 September 2026 with web search, and none of it has been verified on the ground. The following are taken from the sources listed: both sets of coordinates and the resulting separation of about 10.5 km; the finished figure's granite, its height figures, its lotus pedestal, its east orientation across the reservoir, the narrow strip of rock joining it to the cliff, the asisa mudra, the vanished brick image house, the 1951 donor inscription and the five bronzes found below the feet; the unfinished figure's status as a high relief sunk in an alcove and joined along its whole back and head, its missing siraspata, incomplete ear, unpolished robe, undecorated square block pedestal and soles on the natural rock, the seventy-five steps, the ninety-nine caves, the twenty-three early inscriptions, the Bo tree and the reclining image; the master-and-pupil legend in four variants; and the datings attributed to Paranavitana and Dohanian. The heights of the two figures and which is taller are reported inconsistently across sources and are left unresolved. The reading of the name as 'sun eating' and the claim that the first rays of the sun strike the finished face are widely repeated in secondary travel writing without a primary source and are treated as claims, not facts. The district attribution of the second site is unsettled in the sources themselves. Access distances, bus services, ticketing, dress rules and site facilities are from the sources and may be out of date. Not verified at all: drone permissions over either site, whether the resident community at the monastery will allow filming and on what terms, whether direct sun reaches the unfinished ear at any hour, current condition and any scaffolding or conservation work, and whether a long lens can be positioned where the payoff needs it. Five Wikimedia Commons images were found by search API and each was confirmed to exist by a titles query before its URL was written here; two of the five are of the unfinished figure, which is the film's most important object. The fifth image is of the surrounding reservoir landscape and not of either carving site, and its caption says so; that file's own description also carries an incorrect date for the reservoir, which is noted and not relied on.

unknowns: No access, permission or contact has been found or confirmed at either site. Everything here is a research direction.

Drone permission over two sacred sites, one an Archaeological Protected Monument with a ticketed enclosure and one a working monastery, is genuinely uncertain and may simply be refused. The film is written so that it does not collapse if it is: a thirteen-metre figure supplies its own scale from the ground, the payoff is a long-lens sunrise and not an aerial, and the opening approach over the reservoir can be replaced by a ground move without losing a beat.

Whether the incumbent and the resident community at the monastery site are willing to have the unfinished figure filmed, and on what terms, has not been asked. A refusal there removes the film's central object and the idea should be dropped rather than reshaped.

Whether direct sunlight reaches the incomplete ear in the alcove at any hour, and if so at what hour and on what bearing. The payoff cut is built to work either way, but the shot list cannot be fixed without knowing.
Whether a long lens can be placed where the close work on the unfinished surfaces needs it, given the alcove, the steps and the depth of the recess.
Whether the legend is still told at the sites by guides and local people as the sources report, rather than only written about, and in which of its four variants.
Current condition of both figures, and whether conservation work, scaffolding, canopies or a shelter now stands over either of them.
Whether the two sites can be reached and filmed on consecutive clear mornings within one trip, given the road between them and the season.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Chathura's assigned choice; all of its supporting detail, including the historical thread, the datings, the heights and the sun-alignment claim, is desk research from secondary web sources and is unverified. The datings are attributed to the scholars who proposed them and are not treated as settled. No scene or shot is decided here.
